q: For my partner it’s emotionally draining and on the second night we had no option but to run to a 24hour store and buy ready to feed bottles. This isn’t what we wanted, but it’s felt necessary to help her eat. It’s so hard watching my partner upset.

q: I just feel like the true nature of breast feeding is disguised but the guilt of feeling you’re not providing is enormous.

q: Immediately after the birth the midwife placed her on the breast and she latched, we’ve had a nurse come out for support and again she latched. However, as helpful as that is, as soon as they leave we struggle.

q: I’m just so overwhelmed. I feel like I’m losing in all directions.
cx: At 24 weeks, caring for a seriously ill parent while intimacy with her husband falters.

q: I made it clear to my husband that I don’t want my mom, MIL, or anyone else in the delivery room. My husband and I discussed it together, made sure we were on the same page, and agreed that we want the birth to be a private experience between the two of us.

q: I officially hit 40 weeks tomorrow, and for the past two weeks we’ve been receiving nonstop calls and texts asking how I’m doing, whether I’m in labor, and if there are any updates. q: We’ve politely told people that we appreciate how excited they are, but the constant checking in is becoming too much and that we need some space. A few people became upset or offended by that.

q: I’ve definitely learned with this pregnancy to not say a peep about a due date AND ESPECIALLY about having prodromal labor. Giving people too much access to what’s happening just opens multiple doors
cx: Her lesson: share no due date and no early-labour news.

q: This morning, she texted us “I got this off the curb” and send a picture of a stroller. Then she says the seating area has holes and will need a replacement. And it needs to be cleaned up. But a “new one is $900.”

q: I’m not against secondhand items, and everything I’ve purchased for baby so far has actually been secondhand. But trying go give us something that isn’t functional is just strange. For context, I don’t even have a stroller on my registry!
cx: A second-hand shopper herself, she still won't take a broken stroller.

q: I’ve been googling this morning and apparently the recommendation is not to use stroller from before 2015, so I’m going to tell her that we can’t safely use it. I’m just dreading the inevitable pushback.

q: Their response was “Why didn’t she wear a looser dress if it’s a secret?” They also implied that I was taking attention away from my husband’s nephew on his special day.
cx: After back-to-back pregnancies she wore a fitted dress; in-laws gossiped about her bump.

q: I know I shouldn’t feel embarrassed or ashamed of my bump but I must admit the comment made me second guess myself. I just want to exist without eyes on me.

q: She’s been puking and sleeping for 3 weeks straight and I can’t bear seeing her like this. […] I’ve been making her appointments, finding different remedies, making store and restaurant runs to maybe find something she can eat (to no avail), hospital runs, snack and water refills, keeping the house clean, I don’t know what more I can do but I know I wish I could help more.

q: I’m almost 11 weeks pregnant and I feel so trapped inside of my body. […] I have to take a nap daily otherwise I’ll be throwing up at night. i don’t feel like myself at all. I‘m loosing myself slowly but surely, day by day.

q: I know it will all be so worth it in the end and this is all temporary. But the feeling of being trapped and this overwhelming dread will not leave.

q: Stop obsessing about giving birth. It more than likely won't go as planned. It's good to know the most basic things about childbirth but the more you obsess about it and the more elaborate birth plans you make, the more likely you're about to freak out if things don't go as planned. And those breathing techniques they tried to make me do at the hospital just pissed me off more than helped.
cx: Four months postpartum, her first tip: obsessing over birth and detailed plans backfires.

q: Taking care of a newborn is the hard part. When people say"just you see" they don't exaggerate, they are just being a bit cunty about it. It really is that hard.
cx: On the 'just you wait' comments pregnant women hear.

q: Everything you'll read about feeding windows are sleep is a lie. Most newborns sleep terribly […] Night shifts can be exhausting, but they saved us in the first two months.

q: Only me and my husband can calm our baby down, my MIL who offered help before just hands us the baby as soon as he starts crying.

q: And just take people's advice with a grain of salt. Especially older women go crazy when they see babies, and offer a lot of advice despite usually not remembering right what having a baby was like.

q: I think the only reason I’m not traumatized is because I kept my expectations low and trusted the doctors

q: I will be coming with things like chocolate, baby wipes, a nail file, protein bars, electrolytes, a face mask for after and lots of small bits for her comfort before, during and after.

q: I feel like I will be stuck on what to do when she's screaming and crying in pain. I'm pretty scared to see her like that if I'm honest but the game plan for now is to be the brave calm and collected face that she needs to reassure her

q: Is there anything you wish had happened? Anything you wish you planned or discussed beforehand?

q: My wife has been supportive and says it’s okay but I just can’t digest the fact that I’ll miss being there for my first new born.
